articles.title: Itamaraty convoca representante da Embaixada da Argentina após Flávio cruzar fronteira do Brasil com o país vizinho e fugir para EUA | G1
articles.standfirst: Senador embarcou com a família em avião particular que partiu de Puerto Iguazú, na província argentina de Misiones. Flávio deixou o Brasil após ser derrotado por Lula nas urnas e STF determinar que ele entregasse os passaportes à Polícia Federal.
articles.summary: Senador embarcou com a família em avião particular que partiu de Puerto Iguazú, na província argentina de Misiones. Flávio deixou o Brasil após ser derrotado por Lula nas urnas e STF determinar que ele entregasse os passaportes à Polícia Federal.
articles.body:
O Ministério das Relações Exteriores (Itamaraty) convocou a encarregada de Negócios da Embaixada da Argentina no Brasil, María Emilia Cortés, a prestar esclarecimentos sobre o contexto da fuga do senador Flávio Bolsonaro ( PL ) para os Estados Unidos nesta semana.

O governo da Argentina confirmou que o senador embarcou com a família em um avião particular que partiu da Argentina na noite de terça-feira (27).

María Emilia Cortés foi recebida na tarde desta quinta-feira (29) pelo chefe do Departamento do Mercosul do Itamaraty, João Marcelo Galvão de Queiroz, em Brasília.

Na conversa, o embaixador pediu a ela informações sobre a fuga do senador e, segundo diplomatas que participaram da reunião, María Emilia ficou de transmitir o que foi debatido ao governo de Javier Milei .

De acordo com diplomatas, o procedimento é praxe em casos desse tipo e não estão previstos desdobramentos no momento. No entanto, novos passos serão definidos à luz dos desdobramentos das apurações.

Internamente, o governo brasileiro decidiu fechar a posição de que o Brasil quer virar a página sobre a fuga do senador e não dar mais importância ao assunto.

Integrantes do governo já decidiram não entrar em discussões públicas com o governo argentino sobre o episódio.

Flávio Bolsonaro (PL-RJ) desembarcou nos Estados Unidos na quarta-feira (28) após fugir do Brasil com a esposa e as duas filhas.

A rota começou ainda na noite de terça-feira (27), quando Flávio e a família entraram na Argentina após cruzarem a Ponte Internacional Tancredo Neves. A via liga Foz do Iguaçu, no Paraná, a Puerto Iguazú, na província argentina de Misiones.

Segundo a Direção Nacional de Migrações da Argentina, a família cruzou a fronteira às 22h50, pelo horário de Brasília.

O órgão afirmou que os quatro apresentaram documentação válida para a viagem e não tinham nenhum impedimento legal para entrar no país.

Cerca de 40 minutos depois, às 23h30, Flávio e a família embarcaram em um jatinho particular do modelo Gulfstream G400, de matrícula LV-JQW. A aeronave pertence à Baires Fly, empresa argentina que realiza voos privados.

O avião decolou de Puerto Iguazú às 0h22 de quarta. A aeronave sobrevoou o Paraguai, a Bolívia e o Peru, evitando o espaço aéreo brasileiro. Às 5h46, pelo horário de Brasília, o jatinho pousou no aeroporto de Guayaquil, no Equador.

Flávio ficou menos de uma hora em solo equatoriano. O avião decolou novamente às 6h22, com destino aos Estados Unidos.

A viagem terminou às 10h24, horário de Brasília, quando o avião com o senador e a família pousou no Aeroporto Executivo de Fort Lauderdale, na Flórida. O terminal fica na região de Miami.

Flávio deixou o Brasil após o Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) determinar que ele entregasse os passaportes à Polícia Federal.

A decisão foi dada em um processo no qual Flávio e o advogado Willer Tomaz são investigados por lavagem de dinheiro, em um suposto esquema que envolveria empresas de Tomaz e bets.

Os dois confirmam que são amigos, mas negam ser sócios e ter cometido qualquer irregularidade.

Na terça-feira (27), um representante do Departamento de Estado dos EUA informou que o governo americano concederia vistos a Flávio Bolsonaro e à família e permitiria a entrada deles no país.

Uma consulta ao sistema da Alfândega e Proteção de Fronteiras dos Estados Unidos (CBP, na sigla em inglês) mostra que o senador recebeu autorização para permanecer por um ano no país.

Os registros mostram que Flávio foi admitido em uma categoria identificada pelo código "DT".

A sigla é usada para autorizações temporárias no país, geralmente ligadas a questões humanitárias.

O g1 procurou a agência para esclarecer o status migratório do senador, mas não obteve resposta até a última atualização desta reportagem.

A consulta mostrou ainda que Flávio utilizou um passaporte diplomático que havia sido cancelado para entrar nos Estados Unidos.

A Polícia Federal (PF) apontou riscos "concretos e atuais" de fuga ao pedir ao ministro Alexandre de Moraes, do STF, a apreensão do passaporte e a proibição de saída do país de Flávio Bolsonaro.

Na avaliação da PF, três elementos centrais indicavam que Flávio poderia deixar o Brasil sob a justificativa de suposta perseguição política:

a manifestação pública e direta do deputado cassado Eduardo Bolsonaro, recomendando ao irmão que deixasse o país;

a existência de estruturas já estabelecidas no exterior que poderiam viabilizar uma permanência prolongada.

O pedido da PF citou uma declaração de Eduardo Bolsonaro em que ele defendeu que o irmão deixasse o país caso fosse derrotado na disputa pelo Palácio do Planalto.

"Em entrevista concedida recentemente nos Estados Unidos, EDUARDO BOLSONARO, irmão do Senador FLÁVIO BOLSONARO, defendeu publicamente que este deixe o país caso não obtenha êxito no pleito eleitoral. Cabe recordar que EDUARDO BOLSONARO foi recentemente condenado pelo crime de coação no curso do processo", disseram os investigadores.

Flávio Bolsonaro desembarca em aeroporto próximo de Miami em 28 de outubro de 2026 — Foto: REUTERS/Eva Marie Uzcategui

articles.title: Alcolumbre pauta votação da PEC da Segurança Pública para a próxima terça-feira | G1
articles.standfirst: Falta de acordo sobre a redução da maioridade penal fez com que proposta não fosse votada antes do segundo turno das eleições.
articles.summary: Falta de acordo sobre a redução da maioridade penal fez com que proposta não fosse votada antes do segundo turno das eleições.
articles.body:
O presidente do Senado , Davi Alcolumbre (União-AP), incluiu na pauta da próxima terça-feira (3) a votação da proposta de emenda à Constituição (PEC) da Segurança Pública.

O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) condiciona a criação do Ministério da Segurança Pública à aprovação da PEC no Congresso.

🔎 Para ser aprovada, uma PEC precisa ter ao menos três quintos dos votos favoráveis em dois turnos de votação. Ou seja, precisa contar com o apoio de 49 senadores .

A deliberação estava prevista para acontecer antes do segundo turno das eleições, mas um impasse sobre emendas que preveem a redução da maioridade penal levou Alcolumbre a adiar a votação .

A dez dias do segundo turno das eleições presidenciais — onde Lula acabou vencendo o senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) — a oposição apresentou uma emenda para diminuir a maioridade penal para até 14 anos , a depender da gravidade do delito.

Como reação, o líder do PT no Senado, Camilo Santana (CE), apresentou uma alteração para reduzir para 16 anos em casos de crimes hediondos.

Aliados de Alcolumbre afirmaram que a retirada de pauta ocorreu porque nem o governo nem a oposição teriam votos suficientes para aprovar suas as emendas – e o cálculo, neste caso, seria de deixar o assunto para depois.

Apesar da ideia de Camilo neutralizar a proposta da oposição, a emenda apresentada dividiu a bancada do PT. Historicamente, a bancada do PT no Congresso Nacional se posicionou contra a redução da maioridade penal.

Diante da divisão na bancada governista e da proposta da oposição, Alcolumbre retirou o tema da pauta com o argumento de que nem o governo e nem a oposição teriam votos suficientes para aprovar suas as emendas.

Presidente do Senado Federal, senador Davi Alcolumbre (União-AP) — Foto: Waldemir Barreto/Agência Senado

No mesmo dia em que a PEC saiu da pauta do Senado em meio ao racha na bancada governista do Senado, o presidente Lula se posicionou a favor da emenda de Camilo Santana ao ser questionado sobre o tema na sabatina da TV Globo .

"O meu pensamento, enquanto cidadão brasileiro, todo e qualquer crime hediondo, eu sou favorável a diminuir a pena. Para crimes hediondos. Eu sou a favor, sou a favor", afirmou o presidente.

Apesar do posicionamento favorável a mudança sugerida por Camilo, Lula defendeu que esse tema não fosse tratado na PEC da Segurança.

"Primeiro você discute a PEC, aprova a PEC e aí você pode discutir a maioridade penal ou não", disse.

Essa posição também é defendida por governistas, como a líder do governo no Senado, Teresa Leitão (PT-PE).

Caso algum trecho sobre maioridade seja aprovado e o texto precise voltar para a Câmara para aprovação dos deputados, governistas falam em "fatiar" a PEC .

Nesse cenário, a parte que já foi aprovada por deputados e senadores segue para promulgação, enquanto as partes que precisam de análise dos deputados, como a redução da maioridade penal, é enviada à Câmara como um texto separado.

A PEC estabelece na Constituição o Sistema Único de Segurança Pública (SUSP) , com o objetivo de integrar a atuação das forças de segurança no combate ao crime organizado.

De acordo com o texto, União, estados e Distrito Federal poderão criar leis na área de segurança pública, incluindo forças-tarefa intergovernamentais, a organização das polícias e guardas municipais e o sistema socioeducativo.

Outro ponto central da PEC da Segurança Pública é o combate a crimes violentos e facções criminosas.

Entre as medidas está a obrigatoriedade de prisão em estabelecimento penal de segurança máxima ou de natureza especial.

Também ficam proibidas ou restringidas a progressão de regime, a concessão de liberdade provisória, com ou sem fiança, e de saída temporária.

A PEC também permite a expropriação de todo e qualquer bem, direito ou valor econômico envolvidos com as atividades criminosas. As regras valem para organizações criminosas, paramilitares e de milícia privada.

articles.title: Mudança no local de provas da CNH gera reclamações de participantes | G1
articles.standfirst: Provas de carro e moto passaram a ser realizadas no Balneário da Amizade há cerca de um mês. Detran-SP afirma que mudança busca garantir maior controle e transparência e que espaço foi vistoriado.
articles.summary: A falta de banheiros próximos, de bebedouros e de locais cobertos tem gerado reclamações de instrutores de trânsito e candidatos que realizam exames práticos para a CNH.
articles.body:
A falta de banheiros próximos, de bebedouros e de locais cobertos para esperar tem gerado reclamações de instrutores de trânsito e candidatos que realizam exames práticos para a Carteira Nacional de Habilitação (CNH) em Presidente Prudente (SP).

Há cerca de um mês, as provas de carro e moto foram transferidas do Centro de Treinamento de Trânsito (Ceatran), no Jardim Santa Elisa, para o Balneário da Amizade.

Segundo os instrutores, a mudança trouxe dificuldades para quem precisa aguardar a realização dos exames, especialmente em dias de chuva ou de sol intenso.

Eles também apontam transtornos para idosos e pessoas com deficiência (PCDs), que precisam de condições adequadas de acessibilidade e permanência no local.

Em entrevista à TV TEM , o candidato Kayque Luciano Borges afirmou que a estrutura do local anterior facilitava a espera antes das provas, enquanto no Balneário da Amizade é necessário se deslocar para encontrar água e banheiro.

"Porque, no centro em si já tem banheiro, água. Aqui não tem. Lá estava bem melhor. Aqui nós estamos no meio da rua. Algumas pessoas que não têm segurança em si mesmo, aqui já ficam mais nervosos para fazer a prova", relatou.

Já o candidato Miguel Corrêa também apontou dificuldades para esperar a avaliação: "Senti que facilitou em questão da aula em si e a prova, porém a infraestrutura não é muito boa".

Instrutores e candidatos reclamam da falta de estrutura após mudança de local de exames práticos em Presidente Prudente (SP) — Foto: Aceituno Jr./TV TEM

A instrutora de trânsito Tânia Aparecida Franco afirma que o Ceatran oferecia uma estrutura mais adequada para receber candidatos, instrutores e examinadores, com banheiros, água, cantina e cobertura.

"O nosso trabalho já estava totalmente estruturado lá no Ceatran. A gente, quando mudou para cá, já enfrentou chuva, semana passada tinha muito sol, tinha muita pessoa de idade, não tinha lugar para sentar, a cantina aqui do balneário estava fechada. Então, estrutura zero. Não só para nós, para todo mundo, os alunos e até para os examinadores", explicou.

A instrutora também afirmou que a mudança foi comunicada com pouca antecedência e que os primeiros candidatos submetidos ao exame no novo local ficaram mais ansiosos.

"Gera uma ansiedade a mudança do local, porque quando se treina lá [no Ceatran], sabe que vai ser lá. Agora mudou o local, os primeiros que vieram aqui ficaram até mais ansiosos. Gerou bastante ansiedade, gerou bastante reprova também", disse.

Tânia também cita a distância do Balneário da Amizade para candidatos que moram em outras regiões da cidade e dependem de transporte por aplicativo.

Em nota, o Detran-SP informou que os exames práticos de direção em Presidente Prudente passaram a ser realizados no Balneário da Amizade em 30 de setembro de 2026.

Segundo o órgão, a mudança tem como objetivo garantir maior controle, imparcialidade e transparência, após denúncias que apontavam possível interferência de pessoas que não pertencem à autarquia e cobranças indevidas pelo uso do espaço anterior, vinculado a particulares.

O Detran-SP também afirmou que uma vistoria técnica avaliou a infraestrutura e as condições de atendimento do novo local, considerado apto para receber os exames. Conforme a nota, o espaço dispõe de áreas cobertas, água potável, banheiros adaptados, lanchonetes e estrutura para acomodação dos candidatos.

O órgão ainda citou a existência de piso tátil, rampas de acesso e vagas exclusivas para pessoas com deficiência, além de condições de acessibilidade para idosos e pessoas com mobilidade reduzida.

Foi registrada apenas uma manifestação na Ouvidoria relacionada à estrutura do novo local para o atendimento de pessoas com deficiência.

articles.title: Mauro Vieira e Marco Rubio se encontram no G20 e marcam nova reunião | G1
articles.standfirst: Encontro acontece em meio à tensão diplomática provocada pela recusa de Donald Trump em reconhecer o resultado das eleições brasileiras. Cúpula do G20 está marcada para dezembro, na Flórida.
articles.summary: Mauro Vieira e Marco Rubio agendam nova reunião após Trump questionar as eleições no Brasil e Flávio Bolsonaro viajar aos EUA contrariando ordem do STF.
articles.body:
Marco Rubio, secretário de Estado dos EUA, e Mauro Vieira, ministro das Relações Exteriores do Brasil — Foto: Reprodução

O ministro das Relações Exteriores, Mauro Vieira, e o secretário de Estado dos Estados Unidos , Marco Rubio, se encontraram nesta sexta-feira (30). Os dois participam de um encontro de chanceleres do G20, que acontece em Atlanta, no estado da Geórgia, nos Estados Unidos.

Segundo fontes do Itamaraty ouvidas pela GloboNews, o chanceler brasileiro e o secretário de Estado norte-americano conversaram e acertaram um novo encontro antes da cúpula do G20, marcada para dezembro deste ano.

O encontro aconteceu durante a recepção de boas-vindas à Reunião de Ministros das Relações Exteriores do G20. Data e local do novo encontro ainda serão definidos.

O encontro acontece em meio à tensão diplomática provocada pela recusa do presidente Donald Trump em reconhecer o resultado das eleições brasileiras.

O presidente norte-americano também afirmou que falará com Lula, mas, novamente não disse se reconhece a vitória do presidente brasileiro. Questionado sobre quem, para ele, havia vencido as eleições no Brasil, ele respondeu que "não quero comentar isso agora".

👉 O resultado do 2º turno foi confirmado pelo presidente do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), ministro Kassio Nunes Marques, ainda na noite de domingo (25).

Lula (PT) derrotou Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), aliado de Trump, no segundo turno da eleição presidencial no último domingo (25) . O petista recebeu 51,79% dos votos válidos, contra 48,21% do senador, com uma vantagem de 4,4 milhões de votos.

Além disso, outro episódio intensificou a instabilidade entre os dois países. O senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) deixou o país com a família rumo aos Estados Unidos , contrariando a proibição do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF).

Flávio recebeu autorização do governo americano para permanecer por 1 ano no país , segundo aponta consulta ao sistema U.S. Customs and Border Protection - CBP (Alfândega e Proteção de Fronteiras dos Estados Unidos).

Os registros mostram que o senador foi admitido em uma categoria identificada com o código "DT" e que pode ficar no país até 27 de outubro de 2027. O CBP identifica DT como “autorizado a entrar temporariamente” (Paroled). O g1 procurou a agência para esclarecer o status do senador no país, mas não obteve resposta até a última atualização desta reportagem.

➡️ Em uma operação secreta, Flávio Bolsonaro, derrotado nas eleições de domingo, deixou o Brasil após descumprir a ordem do STF.

Segundo as autoridades argentinas, Flávio entrou no país na noite de terça-feira (27) por terra. A PF suspeita, porém, que ele tenha entrado na Argentina em um avião privado;

No território argentino, o senador embarcou em um jatinho executivo com destino aos EUA;

O trajeto evitou o espaço aéreo brasileiro e incluiu uma escala no Equador;

Flávio e família desembarcaram em Miami, às 10h24.

articles.title: Cláusula de barreira: MP apoia somar votos do Avante em nova federação | G1
articles.standfirst: Procuradoria-Geral Eleitoral disse ao TSE que votos do Avante, que não cumpriu a cláusula de barreira nas eleições de 2026, poderão ser somados aos da federação formada por Solidariedade com PRD, que também não cumpriu.
articles.summary: A PGE deu parecer favorável para que o Avante some seus votos à federação do Solidariedade, garantindo acesso ao Fundo Partidário e tempo de propaganda na TV.
articles.body:
A Procuradoria-Geral Eleitoral (PGE) se manifestou nesta quinta-feira (29) favoravelmente a um pedido da Federação Renovação Solidária, formada por Solidariedade e PRD, para que seus votos sejam somados ao Avante, que ingressará na federação, com objetivo de atingir a cláusula de barreira.

O Avante já aprovou em convenção nacional o ingresso no bloco, que também teve o aval da federação em assembleia geral.

Os partidos agora esperam a autorização do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) e pedem que o aval seja dado em caráter provisório antes de 1º de janeiro de 2027, para assegurar o reconhecimento da nova composição antes do início da próxima legislatura.

O professor de Direito Constitucional Gustavo Sampaio, da Universidade Federal Fluminense (UFF), entende que o fato de o partido e a Federação terem concorrido isoladamente nas eleições impede o acesso a recursos do Fundo Partidário.

“Se o partido concorreu isoladamente, se a federação concorreu isoladamente, eu quero acreditar que ela não tendo superado a cláusula de barreira perde acesso ao Fundo Partidário”, afirmou o professor.

“Tivesse sido celebrada [a Federação] por manifestação da vontade de dois partidos ou de uma federação e de um partido esse acordo, durante o processo eleitoral, em tempo de ser homologado pela Justiça eleitoral, eu compreenderia, mas não foi o caso”, ressaltou Sampaio.

Juntos, o Avante e a federação devem chegar ao número mínimo de votos para superar a exigência. O principal efeito seria acesso a recursos do Fundo Partidário e à propaganda de rádio e TV.

Neste ano, para superar a cláusula, cada partido ou federação precisaria ter cumprido pelo menos um de dois critérios:

obter ao menos 2,5% dos votos válidos nacionais para deputado federal e alcançar pelo menos 1,5% dos votos válidos em cada uma de, no mínimo, nove unidades da Federação ou;

eleger ao menos 13 deputados federais, distribuídos por pelo menos nove unidades da Federação.

A federação não alcançou o percentual nacional nem a presença mínima em nove unidades da Federação. Também ficou abaixo dos 13 deputados necessários pelo critério de cadeiras.

Os partidos argumentaram que a circunstância de o Avante ter disputado as eleições separadamente dos demais integrantes da federação não é um problema para a consideração conjunta dos votos.

A Federação argumenta ainda que o resultado das eleições não é alterado, porque os quocientes eleitorais ou partidários permanecem os mesmos, assim como a lista de eleitos e suplentes.

A soma também não atribui a candidato de determinada legenda votos obtidos por outra. O advogado da Federação, Alexandre Bissoli, argumenta que não há proibição legal para ingresso de outro partido no bloco e que a criação da Federação SDD/PRD respeitou o prazo de 6 meses antes do pleito.

Urna eletrônica — Foto: Isadora Pereira/g1

Em parecer enviado à ministra Estela Aranha, do TSE, a procuradoria sustenta que o fato de o Avante ter disputado o pleito separado da Federação impede a soma dos votos para obtenção do quociente eleitoral e partidário, mas não proíbe o atingimento da cláusula de desempenho

A PGE diz ainda que o fato de outros partidos não terem contestado o pedido “depõe em favor da tese” da Federação.

A procuradoria cita uma decisão do presidente da Corte, ministro Nunes Marques, que aceitou um pedido da Federação Rede-PSOL adotando critério de arredondamento no cálculo da cláusula de barreira.

Na oportunidade, o presidente do TSE entendeu que o critério de arredondamento “não interfere nas regras da disputa, não altera votos, candidaturas, quocientes ou a distribuição de cadeiras e repercute apenas na aferição posterior do acesso aos recursos do Fundo Partidário e à propaganda gratuita no rádio e na televisão”.

Para a PGE, os argumentos da Federação SDD/PRD tem semelhança com o que foi decidido por Nunes Marques.

articles.title: Netanyahu's party claims Israel's election was stolen. Now what?
articles.summary: Benjamin Netanyahu, facing a possible election ouster, has made a contentious claim that a foreign country meddled to boost voting by Israel's Arab minority.
articles.body:
Tel Aviv — Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his Likud party alleged Thursday that Israel's election earlier in the week was stolen by Arab-majority parties, helped by foreign funding that amounted to vote-buying, as final results showed Netanyahu's bloc has lost its majority in Israel's parliament, the Knesset.

Israel's Arab-majority parties had their highest turnout ever in Tuesday's election, winning an unprecedented 19 of the Knesset's 120 seats. Their success is one of the main reasons Netanyahu's bloc lost its majority and can't now form a new government.

The final election results show the far-right wing bloc's share of Knesset seats fell from 68 to 53.

Israel's Arab minority, also called Palestinian citizens of Israel, makes up about 20% of the country's population.

"Israel's elections have been stolen," Netanyahu's Likud party declared in a statement Thursday, claiming "an attack on democracy aimed at leading to a foreign takeover of the Knesset, the Islamization of Israel, and the overthrow of the right-wing government to cause a withdrawal and defeat of the IDF (Israeli military) on all fronts — first and foremost, Iran."

The four parties that make up the main bloc opposing Netanyahu won 48 seats, so they would need some support from the Arab parties to try to form a coalition government, assuming none of the lawmakers currently aligned with Netanyahu's bloc defect.

The heads of Israel's two biggest Arab parties, which collectively won 19 seats, have said they would be willing to help the main opposition bloc oust Netanyahu from power.

Most of the Jewish-led parties that oppose Netanyahu vowed before the election not to rely on support from Arab parties to form a government, however, leaving a question mark over whether they might now be willing to cooperate to build a coalition to unseat the incumbent prime minister.

"No basis to the claims regarding a systematic compromise"

The Shin Bet, Israel's internal security agency, said it had opened an investigation into possible foreign influence in the election, but the scope of that investigation has not been made clear.

"An investigation of this type is also focused and bounded, and does not cast aspersions or place blame on an entire sector that went out to vote democratically and legally," the agency said in a Thursday statement.

The Acting Director-General of the Central Elections Committee, Din Livne, said in a letter to a committee member on Thursday that "there is no basis to the claims regarding a systematic compromise of the integrity of the elections."

Israel media reports said one of the allegations the Shin Bet investigation would consider was whether Qatar had sent money to Arab parties in order to increase turnout among Arab Israeli voters.

Qatar's foreign ministry has denied the accusation.

"We categorically deny allegations that Qatar has interfered in Israeli elections or funded any activities intended to influence their outcome," ministry spokesperson Majid Al-Ansari said. "Qatar should not be used as a scapegoat for the political failures of certain Israeli politicians."

While vote counting is now officially complete, the election results must still be certified and sent to President Issac Herzog before a new parliament can be sworn in and the process of forming a new government begins.

Gadi Eisenkot, head of the centrist Yashar party and the top candidate to replace Netanyahu as prime minister, said he was worried that Netanyahu could be using the allegation of a stolen election to justify delaying or disqualifying the results.

"Netanyahu, who has accustomed himself to dealing with reality through lies, consciousness engineering, and the spreading of chaos, is leading alongside his partners an improper influence operation on the Israeli public aimed at delaying the publication of the election results on time and creating fictitious delegitimization of the activity of the 26th Knesset," Eisenkot said Thursday in a social media post.

Once the new Knesset is sworn in — even without a new government decided on — Eisenkot's bloc, along with the Arab parties, could begin passing laws given that they will control a majority in the parliament.

Netanyahu, who President Trump endorsed enthusiastically , will remain in his post as a caretaker prime minister until a new government is formed. If the parties cannot negotiate to form a new coalition government, then the country would have to hold the election all over again, and Netanyahu would remain the prime minister in the interim.

articles.title: Student-loan borrowers in public service are trapped with debt that 'should be forgiven,' a new lawsuit says
articles.summary: The American Federation of Teachers sued Trump for stalling student-debt relief for thousands of borrowers in Public Service Loan Forgiveness.
articles.body:
The Education Department is facing a new lawsuit over the Public Service Loan Forgiveness program.

The lawsuit said the department is failing to process buyback applications and is illegally rescinding borrowers' payments.

These delays are forcing borrowers to pay off loans that should be forgiven, the lawsuit said.

The Trump administration is facing another lawsuit over claims it's mishandling student-loan forgiveness for thousands of borrowers.

On Friday, the American Federation of Teachers President Randi Weingarten filed a lawsuit against the Department of Education over stalled debt relief for borrowers pursuing Public Service Loan Forgiveness , which forgives student debt for government and nonprofit workers after 10 years.

The lawsuit, which is seeking class-action status, said that the department has failed to process the buyback applications of 90,000 borrowers, which allows borrowers to "buy back" months spent in deferment or forbearance if those months would put them at the threshold for relief.

The lawsuit also said the department has illegally rescinded payments borrowers have made toward the program, "trapping in debt borrowers whose loans should be forgiven." It includes Donald Knierim, who previously spoke to Business Insider , as a declarant in the case. Knierim retired after being notified that he had achieved PSLF, only to have 15 of his payments rescinded months later.

Advocacy group Protect Borrowers is representing the AFT. Its senior counsel, Laura Dismore, said in a statement that PSLF borrowers "deserve better than more dysfunction and broken promises."

"The law guarantees public service workers certain rights, and we will enforce those rights wherever and whenever they are violated," Dismore said.

The Department of Education did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Business Insider.

Ongoing Public Service Loan Forgiveness challenges

Business Insider has heard from public service workers over the past who have faced a slew of challenges with PSLF. For example, the PSLF payment tracker has not updated for many borrowers, leaving those who made their final payments waiting for their relief to be processed.

The continued backlog of buyback processing has been an added strain; the department's most recent status report in a separate lawsuit filed by the AFT said that 88,000 applications were pending. The department said some borrowers submitted multiple buyback requests, which inflated the backlog.

More recently, PSLF borrowers like Knierim received notices that the payments they had made toward forgiveness no longer count, extending some borrowers' repayment timelines by years. The department said the clawbacks were due to Biden-era coding errors.

All of the listed delays to relief are actively harming borrowers in public service, the lawsuit said. For example, Elizabeth Schoepflin, one of the plaintiffs, said that the Education Department "ripped away the loan forgiveness credit I earned without any explanation."

"Every month this drags on is another payment I shouldn't have to make," she said.

David Petley, another plaintiff, said he's been waiting over a year and a half for his buyback application to be approved.

"I am expected to keep making more expensive monthly payments in the meantime," he said.

These challenges come as the Trump administration is implementing its student-loan repayment overhaul , which includes new repayment plans and borrowing caps. While borrowers have reported surging monthly bills under the plan, the administration has said its changes are intended to simplify a complex repayment system and curb excessive borrowing.

Have a story to share about student loans? Contact this reporter at asheffey@businessinsider.com .

If you enjoyed this story, be sure to follow Business Insider on Yahoo.

articles.title: Leo XIV becomes first pope to vote in US general election
articles.summary: The Vatican say the pontiff submitted a mail-in ballot in Chicago, citing his long-standing belief in civic participation.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Pope Leo XIV has become the first pope to vote in a U.S. general election, casting a mail-in ballot , the Vatican confirmed Friday.

The Vatican said the Chicago-born pontiff submitted a mail-in ballot in Chicago ahead of next Tuesday's midterm elections, citing his long-standing belief in civic participation.

Leo, formerly Robert Prevost, "has exercised his right to vote as a United States citizen" and has done so "whenever he was eligible to do so," the Holy See press office said.

The statement said he also voted while living in Peru whenever he was eligible. Leo lived in Peru as a missionary priest and bishop for over 20 years.

Leo holds U.S. and Peruvian citizenship, and is also the head of state of a foreign country, the Holy See. The city-state is an absolute monarchy with no political elections.

Pope Leo requested midterm mail-in ballot before his surgery

Leo's vote was first reported by the Chicago Sun-Times , which quoted the chief of staff at the Will County clerk's office as saying the pope, registered at a New Lenox address, requested a mail-in ballot on Oct. 3.

The request was made just 10 days before Leo underwent surgery to remove a cancerous tumor from his right lung. He has slowly resumed his activities at the Vatican after being released from the hospital earlier this month.

It is unclear how Leo returned the ballot. Since 2000, Robert Prevost has voted in five primary elections, requesting Democratic ballots twice and Republican ballots three times, according to records held by the Illinois State Board of Elections.

The records do not show which candidates he supported. Illinois voters must declare a party preference to receive a primary ballot. No such declaration is required in general elections.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Pollsters: Gov. Katie Hobbs opening up lead on Biggs
articles.summary: (The Center Square) – With five days to go until the midterm elections, polling suggests Arizona’s Gov. Katie Hobbs will stick around for another four years.
articles.body:
(The Center Square) – With five days to go until the midterm elections, polling suggests Arizona's Gov. Katie Hobbs will stick around for another four years.

That's the takeaway from multiple polls that show the Democratic incumbent opening her lead over U.S. Rep. Andy Biggs, R-Gilbert, with Cook Political Report's latest batch of gubernatorial polls upgrading the race from "Lean Democratic" to "Likely Democratic."

Elsewhere, Thursday's aggregate polling update from MSNOW and data partner FiftyPlusOne show Hobbs, a former Arizona secretary of state and state Senate minority leader, holding a +8 lead over Biggs, sitting at 49.3% to 41.8% for her Republican challenger.

On Thursday, Jessica Taylor of Cook Political Report said Biggs' efforts in the race have drawn more questions than answers, leaving the party's biggest backers to stay clear of the race entirely.

"Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs began the cycle as Democrats' most endangered incumbent," Taylor said in her latest polling update . "But national Republicans have never been impressed by the race Rep. Andy Biggs has run here, and apart from the Arizona-based Turning Point USA, national GOP groups haven't invested here.

"A HighGround survey this week showed her up by 12 points, 52%-39%, and the margin may not be that large, but she should comfortably win."

To Taylor's point, the Arizona Secretary of State campaign finance page shows that Hobbs' campaign has raised nearly three times as much ($15.044 million) as Biggs ($5.7 million) with Election Day approaching.

Hobbs' late surge speaks to her appeal across Arizona's complicated political landscape, said Thom Reilly, a professor and the co-director of the Center for an Independent and Sustainable Democracy at Arizona State University in Tempe.

"Hobbs has the advantages of incumbency and an established fundraising operation, while Biggs has a different political and ideological profile," Reilly told The Center Square.

Earlier this year, President Donald Trump endorsed Biggs, describing him as a "steadfast Trump ally." The candidate also received endorsements from two former Arizona governors, Republicans Jan Brewer and Doug Ducey.

"Biggs' record in Congress and his close alignment with the MAGA wing of the Republican Party make him a more explicitly partisan candidate, which could be a consideration for independent and moderate voters," Reilly said.

"Voters also have Hobbs's record as governor to evaluate alongside Biggs's congressional record," he added.

Mike Noble, founder and CEO of Noble Predictive Insights, told The Center Square that the state's history of thin voting margins means that writing off either candidate at this point could be a fool's errand.

"Arizona is still Arizona," Noble told The Center Square. "Cook's rating reflects the advantage Gov. Hobbs has shown in public polling, but let's not forget this is a state where statewide elections have been decided by razor-thin margins. A polling lead and an Election Day result are two very different things."

As of Friday morning , Noble's firm has Hobbs up six points on Biggs, sitting with 51% support to 45% for her opponent and putting her just outside the 4.34% margin of error.

When it comes to polling in Arizona, Noble's experience is that the state's electorate tends to go as its largest voting bloc do.

Noble cited that bloc as the turning point in this year's midterms, with Hobbs holding a 62%-to-32% lead among independent voters in Friday's polling update.

"The biggest challenge for Republicans in Arizona isn't necessarily the size of their base. It's what happens with independents," Noble said. "You can have more registered Republicans than Democrats, but if you're losing independents by double digits, that advantage can disappear pretty quickly."

Arizona's sizable independent voter base can produce skewed results, though, Noble said, with Arizonans frequently splitting their ticket or moving between parties depending on what's happening at the time of the election.

"One thing people often overlook about Arizona is how willing voters are to split their tickets," Noble said. "Just because a voter supported Trump in 2024 doesn't automatically mean they're voting Republican for governor in 2026.

"Arizona voters have repeatedly demonstrated that they're willing to evaluate candidates individually, regardless of party," he added.

articles.title: Judge opens East Potomac Park probe into potential DOJ misconduct
articles.summary: A federal judge has opened an investigation into concerns that the Trump administration lied to her in the ongoing legal battle over President Trump’s desire...
articles.body:
A federal judge has opened an investigation into concerns that the Trump administration lied to her in the ongoing legal battle over President Trump's desire to redevelop East Potomac Golf Links.

Friday's hearing became the latest fiery courtroom clash between U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes and the Department of Justice (DOJ), which repeatedly took issue with the judge's lines of questioning and pushed back on any suggestion that information was wrongly withheld.

"The court will open a formal inquiry into whether agency officials and employees, including agency attorneys and DOJ attorneys, have made misrepresentations to the court and otherwise violated ethical rules," the judge said.

A preservationist group and local golfers are suing to stop major redevelopments at East Potomac Park, the longtime home of a public golf course along the edge of the nation's capital. Trump has repeatedly expressed a desire to redevelop it into a championship-style course, and in recent days, he has said the site will close beginning Nov. 15 so the project can proceed.

The president's comments — and recent work to cut down hundreds of trees — have escalated the legal fight.

In a flurry of recent hearings in Reyes's courtroom, the judge whom former President Biden appointed has repeatedly torn into DOJ attorneys about their representations on the status of the project, suggesting they were telling her something different and not to believe the president.

Reyes began on Friday by reminding the DOJ's No. 3 official, Stanley Woodward, about professional ethics rules he is bound to follow as an attorney practicing before the court. As they continued to spar, the judge at one point told Woodward to "finish that thought internally" and to "talk about it at drinks with your friends."

"We're not on TV. I'm not a pundit," Woodward pushed back at another point, also suggesting some of the judge's questioning was blocked under executive privilege.

The judge announced she was opening the investigation after learning that the government has been working to submit the redesign plan to the National Capital Planning Commission, which examines major government projects in the Washington area. Reyes expressed frustration that the DOJ hadn't previously told her about it. She said she'll conduct the investigation herself or appoint a special master to do so.

As of now, the judge has restricted further tree-clearing at the golf course and has implemented new notice requirements, but she hasn't yet outright blocked the planned closure.

"Trust but verify … no longer," Reyes warned the government.

articles.title: Oppn trying to foment anarchy amid global crisis, says Modi
articles.summary: PM Modi in Banaskantha accuses opposition of spreading rumours amid Iran war crisis, vows to serve till last breath, cites fertiliser subsidies and projects.
articles.body: Bhildi (Banaskantha): Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Friday accused the opposition of rumour-mongering and creating panic at a time when the country was unitedly trying to deal with the crisis triggered by the Iran war and the wider Middle East conflict. He alleged that its aim was to foment anarchy across the country and defame him.Addressing a gathering in Bhildi, Banaskantha, after inaugurating the Bharat Bovine Breeding and Research Centre (BBBRC) and launching development projects worth Rs 14,000 crore, Modi said the country was united in working towards the goal of a Viksit Bharat, but some people were unhappy with its progress.“Today every citizen in the country is working towards the dream of Viksit Bharat. In fact, they rejoice when the country is in trouble,” Modi said.He also asserted that he would continue serving the people until his last breath. The remarks came days after Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge’s comment suggesting Modi’s imminent exit triggered a political controversy for his choice of words. Without directly referring to it, Modi declared: “Jeevan ke antim kshan tak janta ki seva main hi juta rahunga (I will continue to serve the people until my last breath).”Referring to the Iran war and the wider Middle East crisis, he accused his political opponents of spreading fears about shortages of fertilisers and cooking gas, and disrupting the lives of ordinary citizens.“When India is unitedly striving to fight the effects of this war, they are spread rumours that farmers won’t get fertilizer, women won’t get gas to cook and children won’t be able to go to school. articles.title: What to know about California’s midterm elections
articles.summary: Redistricting in California, the most populous US state, could flip control of US House from Republican to Democrat.
articles.body:
As voters across the United States head to the polls for the midterm elections – widely seen as a referendum on President Donald Trump’s second term in office – the state of California is set to play an important role.

Several races across the country’s most populous state could help determine whether the Democratic Party takes control of the US House of Representatives, where Trump’s Republican Party currently holds a slim majority.

California’s ballot initiatives – or policy decisions made by voters – have also received national attention.

Perhaps the biggest difference in this year’s elections, however, is the introduction of new congressional district maps drawn up through a partisan redistricting initiative approved by California voters last year.

That initiative aims to net at least five additional Democratic Party seats in the House, where Republicans have a four-seat majority.

Which California races are competitive, who are the main candidates and how has the state’s redistricting push changed the electoral landscape?

The election will be held on Tuesday, November 3. California polls will be open from 7am (15:00 GMT) to 8pm (04:00 GMT Wednesday). Mail ballots must be postmarked by election day.

The House is divided into 435 districts, each represented by one member of Congress elected by their constituents. While congressional districts are populated equally, their boundaries are set by states and can shift.

Partisan redistricting involves states drawing those district maps in a way that advantages candidates from one party over another.

California Governor Gavin Newsom, a Democrat and Trump critic, first proposed a one-time statewide redistricting effort in response to seven Republican-led states redrawing their maps in an attempt to secure seats for Republicans. Although California had banned partisan redistricting, Newsom pitched the idea as an unfortunate but necessary retaliatory measure.

California voters approved the redistricting plan in a 2025 ballot measure – Proposition 50 – that temporarily suspended the state’s nonpartisan redistricting commission until 2030. California then drew new maps to make several Republican strongholds more competitive for Democratic challengers.

As a result, the handful of districts previously seen as favourable terrain for Republicans have instead become hotly-contested races between the two parties.

California has 52 members in the House of Representatives – the most of any state – with Republicans holding just eight of the seats. There are several closely watched state races in the Democratic Party’s effort to secure a majority in the House, the lower chamber of the US Congress.

One is the 22nd congressional district, located in California’s agriculture-rich Central Valley. The district map was redrawn under Proposition 50, setting up one of the state’s most contentious races in a former Republican stronghold.

Incumbent Republican Representative David Valadao is locked in a tight race with Democratic challenger Randy Villegas. Valadao has portrayed himself as a moderate, while Villegas has hammered him over issues such as the rising cost of living, healthcare and Trump’s immigration crackdowns – a key issue for the area’s immigrant farm-working communities.

California’s 48th district, a traditionally Republican stronghold which includes parts of San Diego County near the border with Mexico, is also considered highly competitive after its boundaries were redrawn. The district’s longtime representative, Republican Darrell Issa, decided to retire after the redistricting, with two local officials – Republican Jim Desmond and Democratic San Diego Councilmember Marni von Wilpert – now vying for the seat.

While California’s redistricting aimed to make historically reliable Republican districts more competitive for Democrats, the process has also had some unexpected impacts: Two Republican members of Congress, Representatives Ken Calvert and Young Kim, have found themselves locked in a bitter race against each other after redrawn maps put them in the same district.

Vying to replace Governor Newsom are Republican political commentator Steve Hilton and Democrat Xavier Becerra. Becerra is a former California attorney general and secretary of health and human services during former President Joe Biden’s administration.

Hilton has blasted Becerra for rising crime and homelessness as well as high fuel prices in California, where a gallon (3.78 litres) of petrol costs $5.95 compared with $4.22 nationally, according to the American Automobile Association. Heavily favoured in the Democratic stronghold state, Becerra has sought to associate Hilton with Trump, who is deeply unpopular among Californians.

Polls show Becerra with a strong lead over the Republican challenger. A recent Emerson poll suggested that he was ahead by 27 points.

What ballot initiatives are voters deciding on?

California voters will also weigh in on a handful of policy questions, including a tax on billionaires and whether the state should adopt mandatory voter ID.

Perhaps the most contentious is Proposition 40, a one-time tax on billionaires to help fund healthcare and education. The measure is one of three impacting the state’s ultra-wealthy residents, with the referendums dubbed the “billionaire battle”.

The tax would apply to about 200 of the wealthiest people in California, according to the news website CalMatters. The proposition is opposed by powerful industries and tech titans, who have poured more than $152m into fighting the ballot measure compared with $33m raised in support of the tax, a California public radio station KQED reports.

The measure has drawn opposition from figures such as Google cofounder Sergey Brin, who has given more than $102m to defeat the referendum, as well as Hilton, Becerra and Newsom. Despite being supported by the Democratic Party, Proposition 40 is also being fought by some progressive groups opposed to the one-time tax.

Other progressives such as Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Ro Khanna, a wealthy member of Congress from California’s Silicon Valley, support the referendum.

Two other ballot measures, Propositions 41 and 42, would effectively nullify Proposition 40 if approved by voters.

Another measure, Proposition 39, has also been the subject of fierce debate. If passed, it would require Californians to show government-issued IDs in order to vote.

While supporters say mandatory IDs will bolster confidence in elections by countering voter fraud, studies have found that fraudulent voting is nearly nonexistent in the US.

Critics say that voter ID laws add obstacles to voting by requiring government-issued documents, such as a driver’s licence, that not all citizens hold. They argue that strong safeguards ensuring only eligible voters cast ballots are already in place.

articles.title: Appeals court rules against Trump — again — on California ballots
articles.summary: A split federal appeals court panel again rejected the Trump administration’s bid to set aside 20,000 California ballots it says are likely noncitizens until they can be verified. The 2-1 majority on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit didn’t dispute a lower court’s finding that the list isn’t credible and ruled the…
articles.body:
A split federal appeals court panel again rejected the Trump administration’s bid to set aside 20,000 California ballots it says are likely noncitizens until they can be verified.

The 2-1 majority on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit didn’t dispute a lower court’s finding that the list isn’t credible and ruled the administration’s position would undermine the Constitution.

“As the district court found—and we discern no clear error—there is no feasible way to identify and segregate the ballots of specific individuals without potentially catastrophic effects on the entire system,” the majority wrote in its unsigned opinion.

The majority comprised U.S. Circuit Judge Gabriel Sanchez, an appointee of former President Biden, and U.S. Circuit Judge Mark Bennett, appointed by President Trump.

The other Trump-appointed jurist on the panel, U.S. Circuit Judge Patrick Bumatay, dissented. He warned that California has a “lax system” for ensuring voters are citizens, and ballots can’t be segregated later if fraudulent votes are found.

“Throughout history, federal courts have acted to protect the voting and civil rights of our citizens by enjoining state action that violates the law,” Bumatay wrote. “And common sense also tells us that the federal government shouldn’t have to sit on its hands while a State allows the violation of federal law, especially when the integrity of federal elections is at stake.”

It’s the second time the 9th Circuit panel has split to side against the Trump administration. Last weekend, the administration tried to leapfrog the trial judge and get the panel to immediately intervene in its favor. The panel ruled it didn’t have jurisdiction yet.

This round, all three judges agreed they could proceed to consider the merits. But the majority said the administration’s arguments still fell flat. It sided with California, which takes issue with the veracity of the administration’s list and argues it has no legal obligation to verify voters’ citizenship ahead of Tuesday.

“To be sure, there are countervailing public interests at stake,” the majority wrote. “There is a public interest in maintaining the integrity of elections. But as discussed, the district court found that the risks that noncitizens are voting are, at best, uncertain.”

The Trump administration could now turn to the Supreme Court to try to seek emergency relief or ask the full 9th Circuit bench to step in.

The Trump administration launched the lawsuit earlier this month as it alleged the state was sending ballots to 20,000 likely noncitizens for the midterm contests. California has a universal mail-in voting program where all active voters are sent a ballot.

Election officials across California have already received hundreds of thousands of ballots, court filings show, and the state’s lawyers have conceded a ballot can’t be separated once it is processed.

U.S. District Judge David Carter, an appointee of former President Clinton assigned the lawsuit, in ruling against the administration suggested it could criminally prosecute any people found to have fraudulently voted. The Justice Department has brought a series of voting-related criminal cases in recent weeks in the state.

At a hearing this week, Carter said he was appointing a special master to investigate the administration’s claims of noncitizen voting.

The Hill has reached out to the Justice Department for comment.

articles.title: Appeals court again rejects DOJ’s bid to segregate over 20,000 alleged noncitizen ballots in California
articles.summary: A federal appeals court on Friday rejected the Trump administration’s latest bid to force California to set aside ballots from over 20,000 people it alleges might be noncitizens.
articles.body: A federal appeals court on Friday rejected the Trump administration’s latest bid to force California to set aside ballots from over 20,000 people it alleges might be noncitizens. The “United States has not made the required showing that such extraordinary relief, during an ongoing election, is clearly required by law,” a 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals panel found in a 2-1 ruling. “As the district court found—and we discern no clear error—there is no feasible way to identify and segregate the ballots of specific individuals without potentially catastrophic effects on the entire system.” The dissenting judge, Trump appointee Patrick Bumatay, wrote that what the government had been suggesting is a “modest” remedy. “The federal government and the States can work together. California decided long ago that aliens can’t vote in its elections. Today, the federal government merely seeks to safeguard that decision. We should have let them try,” he wrote. The majority judges were Mark Bennet, another Trump nominee, and Gabriel Sanchez, a Biden nominee. It was the second time in a week the appeals court panel had rejected a request from the administration to intervene in the case. The administration filed suit earlier this month demanding California election officials set aside over 20,000 ballots it contended may have been sent from noncitizens. In a ruling Wednesday, U.S. District Judge David Carter found the request “violates longstanding constitutional principles mandating that states have control over their elections.” “If Plaintiff’s last-minute request for relief were granted, either party could create chaos for their own political purposes to disrupt the election process,” he ruled. Carter also questioned the administration’s methodology in coming up with its list of names, and noted that the Department of Homeland Security had claimed in July that the number of noncitizens who were registered to vote in California was closer to 200,000. “Given the vagueness of Plaintiff’s descriptions of its procedures and the unreliability of its similar claims in other states, the Court cannot conclude that Plaintiff’s process is credible,” the judge wrote. He also pointed to similar claims the administration had made in Nevada, where it had alleged there were 15,903 registered voters as noncitizens. They “later reduced that number to 6,218, and then to 185 after conducting its manual review. Nevada officials later confirmed that all 185 individuals were citizens,” the judge wrote. In its earlier ruling, the appeals court judges also pushed back on the government’s claim it needed to step in on an emergency basis, saying it was “at least in part, a self-constructed one” because it had waited it until far too close to the election to intervene. The Justice Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the ruling or whether it planned to file an emergency appeal to the Supreme Court. Kristen Clarke, general counsel of the NAACP, which was involved in defending the case, said in a statement, “The Department of Justice sought to throw out the voices of more than 20,000 Californians without credible evidence and outside the established safeguards that protect voters’ rights.” “Today’s decision sends a clear message: our elections must be governed by facts, law, and constitutional principles, not political interference or voter suppression,” the statement said.

articles.title: Sabato’s Crystal Ball shifts 2 Senate races toward Democrats
articles.summary: Election forecaster Sabato’s Crystal Ball moved the Senate races in Minnesota and Louisiana toward Democrats in the final days leading up to the Nov. 3 midterms. Louisiana’s race, which it previously rated as “safe Republican,” has now moved to “likely Republican,” while Minnesota went from “leans Democratic” to “likely Democratic,” the forecaster reported Friday. In…
articles.body:
Election forecaster Sabato’s Crystal Ball moved the Senate races in Minnesota and Louisiana toward Democrats in the final days leading up to the Nov. 3 midterms.

Louisiana’s race, which it previously rated as “safe Republican,” has now moved to “likely Republican,” while Minnesota went from “leans Democratic” to “likely Democratic,” the forecaster reported Friday .

In Louisiana, President Trump-endorsed Rep. Julia Letlow (R) is facing off against Democratic candidate Jamie Davis. The Hill’s nonpartisan election forecasting partner, Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), leans the race heavily toward Letlow — whom it gives an overwhelming 88 percent chance of winning.

Though Louisiana is reliably right leaning, Crystal Ball analyst Kyle Kondik wrote Letlow “could be in a tighter-than-expected race” with her opponent, citing early voting data by Louisiana-based conservative pollster John Couvillon showing “excellent Black voter turnout.”

In Minnesota’s Senate race, recent polls placed Democrat Peggy Flanagan double digits ahead of her GOP opponent, Michele Tafoya. DDHQ leans heavily in favor of Flanagan, giving the Minnesota lieutenant governor an 85 percent chance of winning.

Kondik noted that, while Flanagan is underperforming “the margin one might otherwise expect a Democrat to get in a light blue state in a blue wave environment,” her chance of claiming Minnesota’s Senate seat is high.

“But is she really going to actually lose to former sportscaster Michele Tafoya (R)? The chances of that seem smaller than what a Leans Democratic rating conveys,” Kondik said.

Crystal Ball’s latest rating changes its Senate composition projections at 49 Democrats, 46 Republicans and five toss-ups. The forecaster will release its final forecast Monday.

articles.title: Trump fumed at coverage of rally cancellations before ordering the events back on
articles.summary: The decision to cancel relieved some political operatives on the ground, who were happy to hear Trump would be engaging in telerallies that tend to be more s...
articles.body:
Flying on Thursday to South Carolina to headline his 25th midterm rally this month, President Donald Trump and his political team made a decision, according to one of his advisers: Instead of holding an in-person rally this weekend in Kansas — a red state where Republicans appear vulnerable — Trump would deliver his closing argument there over the telephone.

A few hours later, another weekend rally in Iowa was similarly scrapped. It was a dramatic and sudden shift in the president's closing-stretch strategy, which had relied on boosting enthusiasm among his base through an exhausting blitz of conservative districts.

When Trump returned from South Carolina, he told reporters he didn't "feel I have to go to Kansas" because GOP Sen. Roger Marshall was "doing really well."

The decision relieved some political operatives on the ground, who were happy to hear Trump would be engaging in telerallies that tend to be more scripted.

"Thank God," one top Republican official told CNN, speaking on condition of anonymity to avoid alienating the White House. "He hasn't moved the needle anywhere."

Less than 24 hours later, the plans changed again. The rallies in Kansas and Iowa were back on, both now scheduled for Sunday. And the frenetic pace that White House officials had signaled was abruptly ending was now ramping back up.

Speaking at the White House on Friday afternoon, Trump said he'd received calls from friends in Iowa and Kansas asking him to reconsider the cancellations.

"We have a couple of races that are very important," he said. "And they said if you could go it would be better than a telerally. And I tried to talk him out of that and I said, 'What about a telerally?' But they asked me. So I'm going to do two on Sunday."

He also cited Saturday afternoon college football games as a reason for moving his events to Sunday.

Officials said the schedule had merely been rearranged to allow more time for Trump to dial into virtual events. But people familiar with the matter described different motivations to CNN.

After signing off on the changes, Trump had grown irked over the media coverage about his decision to cancel his final rallies, those people said. His irritation was apparent when he returned from South Carolina and lashed out at a reporter who questioned why he called off the events.

"You've been following me for two weeks. I feel perfect," Trump said when asked how he was feeling and whether he was sick of campaigning. The reporter who asked, Trump seethed, looked "like hell."

The president demanded the rallies be reinstated, the people familiar said, sending staff who had just worked to pull the events off the calendar scrambling to put them back on.

"Rallies are BACK ON!" read a statement confirming the change.

The episode only underscored how heavily Republicans' midterm prospects have relied on Trump's personal whims, from endorsements of his preferred candidates — some of whom are now struggling — to his signature rallies, which regularly veer away from the issues and talking points many candidates have tried to highlight.

Even some Republican candidates have scrambled to keep up.

"I think that I'm doing so well in the polls that he's got, probably got better places to spend his time," Marshall told reporters after news of the Kansas cancellation emerged Thursday.

Trump advisers insist the president remains a sought-after presence on the campaign trail, and his political team continues to field calls from GOP campaigns asking if he would visit their states in the sprint to Tuesday's elections, one adviser told CNN.

That was what Trump officials argued was the original rationale for canceling his events this weekend: by skipping in-person events, Trump could maximize his time conducting telerallies for candidates across multiple states. Multiple sources familiar with the planning did not contradict that rationale.

By Thursday evening, Trump's super PAC, MAGA Inc., had announced the president would headline virtual events in 19 states intended to "energize voters, drive turnout, and help deliver victories."

The switch to virtual events was not unwelcome in some Republican corners. In the 21-hour stretch of time that the in-person events were canceled, several GOP operatives in battleground states quietly expressed a sigh of relief that the Trump roadshow would no longer be coming to their states.

Many pointed out that Trump is less likely during telerallies to meander into the obscure topics that now consume major chunks of his rallies: the cognitive tests he claims to have aced, the White House ballroom, the bodies of various Republican men.

One Republican official said the Trump rallies were too time-consuming during a peak period when GOP activists would otherwise be door-knocking, canvassing and doing other get-out-the-vote activities.

Trump has pressed his aides at times to schedule more travel in the campaign's closing weeks, people who have spoken with him said, invigorated by the adoring crowds he's encountered in deep-red districts and encouraged by friends and advisers who have told him his presence is directly boosting Republican enthusiasm.

Yet at other moments during the monthlong barnstorming, those people said, he's bemoaned the breakneck nature of a tour that has taken him to a new town nearly every day — oftentimes to rally voters in college arenas or civic centers that appear downright miniature compared with the sold-out stadiums he played during his own campaigns. Trump has also griped privately, and increasingly in public, about how hard he's having to work down the stretch for a campaign that's not his own.

"I have to tell you a little secret," Trump said during an October 23 rally in a Florida arena that sat fewer than 5,000 people. "Outside, there's a crowd about two or three times this size, and I looked at my people with anger. I said, couldn't you have gotten us a larger arena than this?"

Later, as Trump boasted about the economy, he joked that he was "wasting my time" with the speeches and should just go home and let his accomplishments speak for themselves — a bit that he repeated at subsequent rallies.

The president has visited nearly every state on the Senate battleground map aside from Maine — many more than once. The initial White House decision to cancel the weekend Midwest appearances caused tremendous buzz, but few complaints among party stalwarts.

"Everyone has seen the president who wants to see him," the second GOP official said.

Trump will travel Friday to Daytona Beach, Florida, for a rally with Republican candidates for Senate and governor, and he is expected to spend part of the weekend at Mar-a-Lago, where an annual Halloween party is planned.

Including Sunday's events, Trump will have headlined 28 rallies since the start of October. Even he has acknowledged the schedule is a grind and that it has taken a toll on his voice.

"I don't need to do this. But I have to because if (Democrats) win the midterms, all of a sudden you're gonna see a slide and all of the crap that we talk about," he told a crowd in Kentucky this month. "That's why I'm here working my ass off for you."

articles.title: US appeals court again rejects Trump bid to set aside California ballots
articles.summary: The 9th Circuit Court calls the petition to remove 20,000 ballots from California’s vote count unconstitutional.
articles.body:
For the second time in less than a week, a United States appeals court has rejected a petition from the administration of President Donald Trump to set aside 20,000 ballots in California over concerns about non-citizen voting.

The decision came down on Friday, with less than four days until the November 3 midterm elections.

The 9th Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that Trump’s request would violate the US Constitution and risk disenfranchising eligible voters.

“The consequence of the United States’s request is not merely ballot segregation, but ultimately both the cancellation of the ballot and the removal of voters from the voting rolls,” the majority wrote in its ruling.

Judges Mark Bennett and Gabriel Sanchez – appointed by Trump and his Democratic predecessor Joe Biden, respectively – formed the majority.

A third judge, Trump appointee Patrick Bumatay, issued a dissent, saying the administration’s petition was a “reasonable request”.

The Trump administration has claimed that nearly 20,000 “likely non-citizens” received mail-in ballots to vote in California’s midterm elections on November 3. It sued the state on October 15 to prevent those ballots from being counted.

But the accuracy of the Trump administration’s list has been called into doubt, as have its claims of widespread non-citizen voting.

Election fraud in the US is extremely rare. So is non-citizen voting, despite Trump’s assertion earlier this year that as many as 278,000 foreign nationals across the country were registered to vote.

Like California, states such as Nevada and Washington have also received lists of alleged non-citizen voters, but officials there have found the documents largely inaccurate.

In Nevada, for instance, state authorities issued a statement in September saying the Trump administration had erroneously identified citizens as non-citizens on its list. Not a single name was correct, according to the statement.

California, a Democratic stronghold, will elect 52 members of the House of Representatives, one of Congress’s two chambers, on November 3.

The state has long been Trump’s target for criticism, with the president accusing its Democratic leadership of “cheating” in elections.

But California officials, including Governor Gavin Newsom, have countered that the Trump administration is seeking to meddle in the state’s elections to sow voter distrust and undermine the results.

“This is a sad, desperate attempt by Trump to use his politicized Justice Department to try to suppress California voters,” Newsom said in a news release after the October 15 lawsuit.

Non-citizen voting in federal elections is against the law in all 50 US states, including California.

The Constitution’s Elections Clause also grants states exclusive authority to administer elections, though it does allow for Congress to pass regulations concerning voting procedures.

The Trump administration initially sent California its list of 20,000 “likely non-citizens” on October 12, barely three weeks before the midterm election.

California officials refused the administration’s demand to set aside the 20,000 ballots, requesting proof that the names on the list were indeed foreign nationals. According to the California government, no such evidence has been provided.

The Trump administration last week charged 28 foreign nationals in California with election-related infractions, but some of the accused told the Los Angeles Times they had never registered to vote.

The newspaper’s reporting suggested some of the non-citizen defendants shared the same name as eligible voters.

As the October 15 lawsuit navigated the court system earlier this month, the Trump administration sought an emergency ruling from the 9th Circuit Court to suspend the 20,000 ballots.

But the appeals court rejected the petition on Monday, saying the Trump administration had not given lower courts adequate time to weigh the matter.

A lower court ultimately ruled against the Trump administration on Wednesday, and the administration again appealed to the 9th Circuit Court.

In its majority decision, the appeals court framed the Trump administration’s lawsuit as an attempt to violate the Constitution’s Elections Clause.

“We decline the United States’s invitation to contravene the Elections Clause by undermining the Constitution’s plain text,” the majority wrote.

The majority also wrote that it had “major concerns” that granting the Trump administration’s request would “harm the public interest by risking the disenfranchisement of eligible voters and putting the entire tabulation process in jeopardy”.

articles.title: The final countdown: From the Politics Desk
articles.summary: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.
articles.body: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, we have the latest midterm campaign trail updates from our reporters in the field. Plus, Kristen Welker shares the top Senate races she will be watching Tuesday. — Adam Wollner The final countdown With the midterm elections reaching their conclusion in just four days, NBC News reporters are spread out across the country, speaking with candidates, operatives and voters about the dynamics shaping the biggest races on the map. Here are our latest dispatches from the campaign trail. Ohio governor: The fallout from Republican Vivek Ramaswamy’s campaign ad featuring the estranged mother of his opponent, Amy Acton, has been a galvanizing moment for Democrats in a state that became redder with President Donald Trump’s rise in politics after a long run as one of the nation’s most competitive battlegrounds, Henry J. Gomez reports from Liberty Township. A private poll paid for by a Republican group this week showed Ramaswamy trailing Acton by 8 percentage points — a 6-point drop from an earlier survey, said a GOP strategist who works on Ohio races. Similar numbers have rattled around Republican circles for days. Michigan Senate: During a campaign event for Republican Mike Rogers, Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, described Democrat Abdul El-Sayed — who, if elected, would be the first Muslim senator — as “a theocratic zealot” and “jihadist leprechaun” whose election would put American service members at risk because, if presented with national secrets, he would be likely to share them with terrorist groups. Cruz, like other Republicans, sought to link El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood, a group the Democrat has condemned. As Allan Smith writes from Grosse Pointe Woods, Cruz’s message has become a staple of the anti-El-Sayed messaging, with Republicans leaning into the theme in advertising and at campaign events. And they’ve been echoed by some voters. Georgia governor: While the Southern battleground has two marquee contests on the ballot next week, only the race for the state’s top job between Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms and Republican Rick Jackson remains tight. In the Senate race, polls broadly show Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff with a sizable lead over his Republican challenger, Rep. Mike Collins. Bottoms and Jackson both have their eye on winning over a potentially critical slice of the electorate that is supporting Ossoff in the Senate race in the final stretch of the race, Adam Edelman reports from Atlanta. Bottoms has campaigned alongside Ossoff and run ads touting his endorsement, while Jackson has backed away from casting himself as a staunch ally of Trump as he did during his GOP primary. New Hampshire Senate: Trump has spent nearly every day this month crisscrossing the country to turn out Republican voters in tight Senate races. But he’s steered clear of the Granite State, which he lost in all three presidential contests. Republican John E. Sununu is reminding the state’s fiercely independent voters that he is not tied to Trump, Brennan Leach and Julie Tsirkin note from Rye. He tells voters in a direct-to-camera TV ad released this month: “I’ve never even met the man!” Closing message: On the airwaves, Democratic Senate candidates have been far more likely to reference corruption, high costs and Trump, while Republicans have been more focused on immigration, crime and transgender issues. That’s according to an analysis from Bridget Bowman of more than 600 TV ads that launched in October. The key Senate races I’m watching on election night Analysis by Kristen Welker Can Democrats turn their recent momentum in red and purple states into a Senate majority? While the battlefield has expanded in recent weeks, here are the races I will be keeping a particularly close eye on next Tuesday. Michigan: The contest between Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers will be a critical test of whether a progressive candidate can win in a swing state as Democrats start to fix their eyes on 2028. President Donald Trump won Michigan by less than 1 percentage point in 2024, but voters in a state driven by the auto industry are grappling with high gas prices and costly trade wars with neighboring Canada. Still, Michigan represents one of Republicans’ few pickup opportunities, and if they are able to flip it, that would give them a major boost as they try to maintain Senate control. Ohio: Sen. John Husted, who was appointed to the seat previously held by Vice President JD Vance, is facing off against former Sen. Sherrod Brown, a Democrat who is on a comeback tour after losing to GOP Sen. Bernie Moreno in 2024. The race has been affected by the governor’s contest, where Republican Vivek Ramaswamy ran that controversial ad featuring Democrat Amy Acton’s estranged mother. The ad, which is no longer running, was met with bipartisan backlash. But could it still serve as a drag on Husted? Texas: Trump’s endorsement power will be put to the test in the Lone Star State. He ignored concerns from Republicans that GOP Attorney General Ken Paxton would be a weak general election candidate and endorsed him over Sen. John Cornyn in the primary runoff.Since then, Republicans have poured hundreds of millions of dollars into defending the seat. If James Talarico manages to flip it, it will be the first time Democrats have won a Senate seat in Texas in more than three decades. Despite winning Texas by nearly 14 points in 2024, Trump has made three trips to the state this month alone. Alaska: There’s a chance control of the Senate could come down to Alaska — and if that happens, it could be several weeks before we know the outcome, given ranked choice voting and the pre-emptive legal challenges developing there. State and federal investigations are now underway after The New York Times reported that Democratic operatives were involved in recruiting a second Dan Sullivan to appear on the ballot in an effort to pull votes away from incumbent Republican with the same name. Democrat Mary Peltola and her campaign have denied being involved in the effort. This Sunday on “Meet the Press,” Steve Kornacki will join me to break down the results of the last NBC News poll before Election Day. I’ll also interview Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., the chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee; Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md.; and Illinois Democratic Gov. JB Pritzker. That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner and Lauren Zola. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here.
