articles.title: Bessent alleges anti-fraud guardrails are ‘loosest’ in blue states
articles.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent accused Democratic-led states Friday of having poor fraud prevention mechanisms while at a Minnesota press conference. The state has been at the center of a healthcare fraud scandal for much of this year after the Justice Department indicted more than a dozen people on accusations of defrauding taxpayers, using funds for…
articles.body:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent accused Democratic-led states Friday of having poor fraud prevention mechanisms while at a Minnesota press conference.

The state has been at the center of a healthcare fraud scandal for much of this year after the Justice Department indicted more than a dozen people on accusations of defrauding taxpayers, using funds for improper billing and childcare fraud, among other allegations.

And while Minnesota is not the only state the Trump administration targeted with fraud investigations, it has become a focal point of its anti-fraud agenda.

“In Minnesota, alongside other senior U.S. officials, U.S. Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent today announced several initiatives to combat the rampant fraud that has wasted billions of dollars in Minnesota,” a release from the Treasury Department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network said.

Bessent accused Democrats of letting fraud happen in states they govern, though he acknowledged such crimes also occur in red states.

“The Democrats [have] let this happen on their watch,” Bessent said. “It’s going on everywhere, and we’re going to track them down. But I can tell you that the guardrails tend to be loosest in the Democratic states.”

A congressional study published in 2023 found that Texas, a red state, had the most Medicaid fraud dollars in 2022 with $219.9 million, followed by California, Florida and Louisiana.

Bessent responded to a question about why they were singling out Minnesota, saying that per capita, the state has been one of the worst at fraud oversight. He placed the blame for this “lack of oversight” on Gov. Tim Walz (D) and his administration.

“The kind of egregious nature of this and the lack of oversight from the AG’s office and from the Walz administration is shocking,” Bessent said. “Minnesota, unfortunately, because of the lack of oversight, likely has as a percent of the dollars one of the largest in the country.”

A Walz spokesperson did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment.

The Trump administration has punished blue states over fraud accusations, freezing more than $1 billion in Medicaid funds for Minnesota and California this summer.

Earlier this year, Vice President Vance began chairing the White House’s anti-fraud task force, aiming to coordinate a national response to fraud at the local and state level. Trump said Vance would focus primarily on blue states in his role as “fraud czar.”

“His focus will be ‘EVERYWHERE,’ but primarily in those Blue States where CROOKED DEMOCRAT POLITICIANS, like those in California, Illinois, Minnesota (Somalia beware!), Maine, New York, and many others, have had a ‘free for all’ in the unprecedented theft of Taxpayer Money,” Trump wrote on Truth Social in April.

Last week, Trump announced a $25 million whistleblower program promising cash payments to those whose tips about fraudsters lead to convictions.

articles.title: 'Biscuit' the dog is latest dead felon to get their voting rights back from Spanberger, confused owner says
articles.summary: A deceased Goochland County beagle named Biscuit reportedly received a Virginia rights restoration certificate, prompting calls for an audit.
articles.body: A Southside Virginia lawmaker is demanding an investigation after a constituent received an official rights-restoration certificate for his dog, Biscuit, a beagle-hound mix from Goochland County that died about five years ago. The discovery follows the "Betty No Last Name" controversy in Chesapeake — where a purported convict lacking a surname had "her" rights restored — and raises fresh questions about the governor's vetting process just days before voters decide whether to make felons' voting-rights restoration automatic via an Election Day ballot measure supported by Richmond Democrats. Del. Tom Garrett, R-Buckingham — who received the letter from the constituent who owned the pet — is now calling for an investigation into how Gov. Abigail Spanberger could have restored voting and jury-service rights to a deceased animal. DEM AG'S ELECTION CRUSADE AGAINST TRUMP RUNS INTO EMBARRASSING DEAD-FELON BLUNDER BACK HOME "This is not a question of whether people who have served their sentences deserve a second chance. This is a question of whether the Commonwealth is exercising one of the Governor’s constitutional powers with even the most basic level of review," Garrett said. "Biscuit was a dog. Biscuit has been dead for five years. Yet an official document bearing the governor’s signature says the executive reviewed the particulars of Biscuit’s criminal case and determined her rights should be restored. Virginians deserve an explanation for how that is possible." HIDDEN CALIFORNIA DESERT PET CEMETERY HOLDS UNEXPECTED PIECE OF WHITE HOUSE HISTORY Biscuit’s owner, who declined to be identified to avoid political backlash, confirmed the letter's authenticity to Fox News Digital and told Garrett in a statement that the pup was a "good dog and is greatly missed." "To my knowledge, she was never convicted of a felony, nor did she ever show any interest in voting," the owner said. Fox News Digital reached out to Spanberger for comment. A spokesperson for Spanberger replied, "Of course we did not restore the rights of a dog. We cannot disclose this individual's information, but we can tell you that it is associated with a person with a date of birth and Social Security number." Fox News Digital followed up to seek clarification on what error may have occurred but did not receive a response. The owner told Fox News Digital that Biscuit was never sent to the pound or had any other contact with Richmond that could have resulted in her being placed on the voting rolls. The owner said a sibling is currently incarcerated but added that the connection is moot because Spanberger’s stated effort only involves released former convicts. ELECTION DAY 2026: JOIN AMERICA'S CONVERSATION HERE! Garrett noted in a statement that the Spanberger administration said in July that Secretary of the Commonwealth Candi Mundon-King would be "proactively identifying Virginians who had lost their rights, confirming that those individuals were eligible, and restoring their rights," in his words. Spanberger announced in August that the initial figure of 66,000 had reached 100,000 individuals who had received restoration of their rights since the Democrat took office in January. TREASURY HAILS SUCCESS OF ANTI-FRAUD PROCESS THAT FLAGGED AND PREVENTED $99 MILLION IN PAYMENTS TO DEAD PEOPLE "The administration told Virginians these individuals were being identified and their eligibility confirmed," Garrett said in a statement, going on to call for an investigation into how a restoration certificate bearing Biscuit's name came to be issued. "The document itself represents that the executive reviewed the particulars of each case. If a deceased family pet made it through that process as a convicted felon, then we need to know what was actually reviewed, what databases were used, what safeguards existed, and how many other erroneous restorations were issued." An attorney in Fluvanna County when not legislating, Garrett said the Commonwealth must launch an immediate independent audit of Spanberger’s restoration-of-rights actions and disclose the underlying record that led to "Biscuit Rigsby" being identified as a convicted felon, as well as what Spanberger’s office defines as the "review of the particulars" of Biscuit’s case. Any investigation should also identify how many certificates and citations were issued to deceased, nonexistent or duplicate humans and require the immediate preservation of relevant data. WATCHDOG, GOP LAWMAKER WARN NY VOTER REGISTRATION SYSTEMS LACKS KEY SAFEGUARDS He said in a statement that his questions are not partisan and that Virginians who support restoring released felons’ voting rights should be outraged by Biscuit’s case. "At what point does rank incompetence and malfeasance become criminal conduct?" Garrett added in a video posted to social media. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP With Virginians set to vote Tuesday on whether to make voting-rights restoration automatic upon release from incarceration, Garrett is demanding answers about the administration's existing review process — including how a dog that died five years ago apparently made it through.

articles.body:
GOP grip on Ohio, Texas in jeopardy amid data center fervor

The importance of AI data centers is growing this election cycle as the fight over the infrastructure’s costs and environmental impacts may be threatening Republicans in battleground states like Texas and Ohio .

Grassroots movements in rural communities, particularly where President Trump won by double-digit margins in each of his presidential bids, are threatening the rural vote the GOP has counted on for decades, experts and voters say.

The debate is ongoing in communities like Pickaway County, Ohio — which Trump won by around 50 points over former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024, and where residents are airing their opinions on EdgeConneX’s latest data center.

“That’s weighing heavily, especially with the Senate races,” Pickaway County resident Sherri Fahringer, who is running for county commissioner, said regarding the data center issue.

Data centers are increasingly being built in rural communities, with 67 percent of planned projects slated in rural areas, according to an April Pew Research Center study.

Welcome to The Hill’s Technology newsletter , we’re Julia Shapero and Miranda Nazzaro — tracking the latest moves from Capitol Hill to Silicon Valley.

Did someone forward you this newsletter? Subscribe here.

How policy will be impacting the tech sector now and in the future:

Top Science Democrat probes cuts to research spending at National Science Foundation

A key Democrat is looking into a massive amount of money that was appropriated to the National Science Foundation (NSF) but reportedly not spent. In a letter first shared with The Hill, House Committee on Science, Space and Technology ranking member Zoe Lofgren (D-Calif.) accused the foundation of violating “Congress’ power of the purse and the rightful separation of powers in our constitutional system” after a report that …

Meta settles with second plaintiff during trial over social media addiction

Meta settled a social media addiction lawsuit with an 18-year-old plaintiff on Friday, avoiding its next bellwether trial, which began jury selection this week. The case, filed by a woman from Mississippi dubbed “K.D.B.,” alleged her use of Instagram and Snapchat as a child worsened her mental health and contributed to her eating disorder, suicidal thoughts, depression and self-harm. K.D.B.’s case against …

Gen Z trusts elections, but not Washington

For younger voters, election-related corruption is less of a concern than for older generations. Four percent of Gen Zers say they’re worried about election fraud and cheating ahead of the midterms, compared with 14 percent of millennials, 21 percent of Gen Xers and 23 percent of baby boomers, per a CBS/YouGov poll.

News we’ve flagged from t he intersection of tech and other topics:

Google’s first data center satellite is online and writing poetry ( TechCrunch )

Big Tech’s data center bliz is burning through cash and scaring Wall Street ( The New York Times )

North Korea linked to $6.3B Binance hack

A North Korea-based cybercrime group appears to be behind a $6.3 billion hack of the cryptocurrency exchange Binance, according to two blockchain intelligence firms.

Both TRM Labs and Chainalysis tied the largest crypto hack on record to TraderTraitor , a North Korean hacking unit that has previously targeted the digital asset industry.

Billions of dollars’ worth of crypto began moving out of Binance wallets on Thursday afternoon. The company quickly suspended all deposits and withdrawals, and crypto firms froze about $3 billion in assets tied to the incident.

The attacker moved approximately $6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on XRP Ledger, Ethereum, Bitcoin, Tron, Solana and several other blockchain networks, with much of this occurring over the span of around 20 minutes, according to TRM Labs.

While the industry managed to freeze a significant portion of assets, the attacker still controls $2.4 billion “beyond any issuer’s reach,” the blockchain intelligence firm noted.

articles.title: Cruz warns GOP could lose 8 Senate seats, get swept in Texas
articles.summary: Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) is warning that Republicans could lose as many as eight Senate seats in the midterm elections and get swept in all of the statewide Texas races, including the Senate contest between Republican Ken Paxton and Democrat James Talarico, if the GOP has a bad day on Nov. 3. “The election is…
articles.body:
Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) is warning that Republicans could lose as many as eight Senate seats in the midterm elections and get swept in all of the statewide Texas races, including the Senate contest between Republican Ken Paxton and Democrat James Talarico, if the GOP has a bad day on Nov. 3.

“The election is just a few days away, and all across the country there are Senate races that are incredibly close. There are eight to 10 Senate races across the country that are basically tied,” Cruz said on a Friday episode of his podcast, “The Verdict with Ted Cruz.”

“If we have a good night on Election Day, we could have a fantastic result. We could end up with 53 Republicans in the Senate. We could end up growing our majority in the Senate,” he said.

But he warned “if we have a bad day” Republicans “could wake up the day after Election Day, instead of 53 Republicans, with 45.”

“That big a delta is at play,” Cruz said after traveling to Georgia, Texas, South Carolina, North Carolina, Michigan and Iowa to campaign for GOP candidates.

Cruz said there will be “massive Democratic turnout” in the midterm elections and warned that Republicans face a potential “bloodbath” if Republicans don’t turn out to the polls in big numbers.

“I’m worried,” he said. “What we’re seeing across the country is massive Democrat turnout.

“Democrats are showing up, they’re energized, they hate, hate, hate Donald Trump,” he said. “If the election were over today, if just the early votes that have been cast so far are counted, Republicans would lose massively.”

But Cruz argued “there are Republican votes out there to turn that around” if GOP-leaning voters get motivated to vote.

He said reliable Democratic voters are showing up “in massive numbers.” But he said the reliable Republican voters aren’t voting early at the same rate as stalwart Democrats.

“Please, please, please show up and vote,” Cruz pleaded to his listeners.

He said there are more reliable Republican voters in the GOP-leaning Senate battleground states, but they need to cast their ballots to make a difference.

Cruz warned that the statewide races in Texas are extremely close and warned that Republicans could get swept in the Lone Star State if things go wrong for their party.

“Texas is excruciatingly close. Understand we could lose Texas,” he warned. “Not just the Senate race. We could lose every single statewide race in Texas. That’s how close these numbers are.”

He countered Republicans who argue the polls are wrong by saying while pollsters may show left-leaning bias on occasion, the data showing huge Democratic turnout this year is very real.

“I can tell you having run a lot of campaigns, having examined a lot of numbers, these data are not fake. The Democrats are massively out-turning out the Republicans. We got to fix that.”

articles.body: The Trump administration asked a federal judge Friday to issue an order before Monday directing Alaska election officials to segregate all ballots ranking Senate candidate Dan J. Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward wrote in a court filing that state officials should “preserve and segregate all ballots ranking Daniel J. Sullivan for the purposes of investigating whether such ranking was the product of voter confusion, should such an investigation become necessary.” “These modest precautionary measures will be impossible after Election Day, so there is good cause for expedited consideration,” he added. The filing did not spell out a process for ballot review or explain how reviewing a ballot would show if a voter was confused about ranking the candidates. Alaska uses ranked choice voting, and there are four Senate candidates on the ballot. The Trump administration has ramped up its efforts to inject itself into the Alaska election, which by statute is handled by state officials, after The New York Times reported this week that Democrat Mary Peltola’s campaign was involved in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan, a former school teacher, to run against Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan. Peltola has denied any involvement in Sullivan’s campaign. Woodward, alongside Alaska’s top federal prosecutor, U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman, made three other filings Friday regarding the civil case the administration is pursuing in hopes of blocking Alaska from certifying the Senate election results. In one filing, the prosecutors requested expedited sharing of “internal and external conversations” from Peltola’s campaign “regarding its efforts to recruit Daniel J. Sullivan to run for office.” Another filing asks for the “Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee’s internal and external conversations regarding its efforts recruit Daniel J. Sullivan to run for office.” The DSCC has said it was “not involved with Dan J. Sullivan.” An additional filing seeks a preliminary injunction in the case. Friday’s filings came shortly after Heyman held a press conference in Alaska, where he acknowledged a parallel criminal case. Asked what potential crimes prosecutors are looking into, Heyman declined to provide details. “Because this is an ongoing investigative matter, we can’t discuss the specifics of those investigative steps, and who or may or may not be involved,” he said. “This protects the integrity of the investigation and it protects those who may be the subject or target of those investigations.” Heyman cited the recent reporting from The New York Times, saying the “new information has resulted in a significant surge of law enforcement assets to Alaska.” The Justice Department issued at least three dozen new subpoenas and document preservation requests as of Thursday, including subpoenas sent to the campaign offices of Peltola and of Dan J. Sullivan. President Donald Trump, who has urged legal action against Peltola and the second Sullivan, said Friday morning that he doesn’t know whether Sen. Dan S. Sullivan can win with the current ballot. “I will tell you, he’s a great senator, and what they tried to do, and he would, you know, he would have won,” Trump said in an interview with Kansas City talk radio host Pete Mundo. “I don’t know how he can win here because you’re splitting up the vote illegally. I think it’s a total fraud.” Trump has said repeatedly that Dan J. Sullivan should be removed from the ballot. In an interview with Fox News’ Sean Hannity earlier this week, Sen. Sullivan told supporters in Alaska how to mark up their ballot to best help him on Election Day. “So rank me first, Sullivan, Dan S. Registered Republican incumbent. That’s what the ballot says,” he said. “Rank the other Republican second, [Gerald] Heikes. articles.body:
FDA unveils proposals to update infant formula nutrient requirements

The Food and Drug Administration is proposing to update nutrient requirements for infant formula, the first nutrition review for formula in nearly 30 years.

The review is part of the Trump administration’s Operation Stork Speed initiative, which was announced in March 2025 as part of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s Make America Healthy Again movement.

“Parents deserve confidence in every bottle they feed their baby” Kennedy said in a statement. “We will hold infant formula manufacturers to rigorous scientific standards and put babies’ health first.”

The proposed rule — which is the first phase of the formula review — would update requirements for vitamin A, vitamin D, iodine and manganese as well as reaffirm existing requirements for chloride, potassium, selenium and sodium.

The review is being conducted in three phases , acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantis said, with the goal of releasing one final rule that will cover all 30 nutrients currently required, as well as potentially additional nutrients.

Personal injury and product liability attorney Bill Marler welcomed the update as long overdue and applauded the additional transparency, but noted the absence of a crucial issue that recently plagued the infant formula supply.

Nothing in the announcement “touches the hazard that actually put American babies in intensive care this year and last,” Marler wrote in a blog post.

“The words Clostridium botulinum do not appear in it. Neither do Cronobacter, Salmonella, nor the word pathogen. “

Since November 2025, 52 infants have been hospitalized with botulism after being fed powdered infant formula.

“Not one of them was hurt by a heavy metal or an outdated vitamin D requirement,” Marler said.

articles.title: Time to set back the clocks, much to Trump’s chagrin
articles.summary: Tick tock – clocks in America will fall back this Sunday. It could be the last time, if President Trump and some like-minded lawmakers get their way. But the debate over making daylight saving time permanent has proven divisive even within the president’s party. The House passed the Sunshine Protection Act earlier this year, which…
articles.body:
Tick tock – clocks in America will fall back this Sunday. It could be the last time, if President Trump and some like-minded lawmakers get their way. But the debate over making daylight saving time permanent has proven divisive even within the president’s party.

The House passed the Sunshine Protection Act earlier this year, which would end the semiannual clock change, but the Senate has yet to pick it up.

Trump has been a big proponent for the permanent change, slamming the Senate for “letting the Daylight Saving Bill die, when a vast Majority of the Country want it.”

“Most people are demanding light in the evening, but ALL want not to change their clocks anymore,” he wrote on Truth Social earlier this week. “TAKE A VOTE!”

Congress isn’t currently in session, and won’t be back until after the clocks change.

At his Mississippi rally on Monday, Trump called the clock change “ridiculous” and said it “drives everyone crazy, which nobody wants to do anymore.”

He pointed to data showing less crime is committed when there’s more light in the evening. Earlier this month, he argued the setback “costs our Country a fortune, is bad for Crime, stress on people, Sports, and just about everything else you can imagine.”

But voices on both sides of the debate can cite data proving their case.

Rep. Mary Gary Scanlon (D-PA) and Rep. Pat Harrigan (R-NC) introduced bipartisan legislation in July called the Sunshine for Our Kids Act that would establish a permanent standard time (the current norm from November to March).

They worry more sunlight in the evenings leaves mornings dark for schoolchildren and commuters.

“For decades, scientists and medical professionals have highlighted the detrimental mental and physical health impacts of twice-a-year clock changes, particularly on children and teens,” Scanlon said in a statement .

At least one Republican agrees with them: Sen. Tom Cotton (R-Ark.), typically a staunch Trump supporter.

“No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent Daylight Savings Time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter,” he wrote in a post on X earlier this month. “Arkansans don’t want their kids going to school in the pitch dark, and I’ll always put Arkansas first.”

An AP-NORC poll from last October found that 12 percent of U.S. adults favor the twice-a-year change, while 47 percent oppose it and 40 percent are indifferent about it.

Some 56 percent said they would prefer daylight saving time year-round, while 42 percent said they would rather standard daylight time year-round.

The golfing industry is a leading proponent of the argument that more daylight in the evenings is better for business – and the economy generally, with more people staying out after work and school.

“Overall, permanent DST is viewed as more beneficial to the golf industry, particularly for small business revenue, accessibility to the game, and general recreational enjoyment and benefits,” National Golf Course Owners Association CEO Jay Karen testified before a Senate committee last year.

“Our industry is uniquely tied to daylight, and the number of playable hours directly affects the number of rounds we can offer, the staff we employ, and the revenue we generate, especially in the late afternoon and early evening.”

An analysis from JP Morgan Chase Institute found that in Los Angeles, when compared to a city like Phoenix that does not observe daylight saving, debit card spending per capita rose at the beginning of daylight saving by 0.9 percent. However, spending dropped 3.5 percent following the end of daylight saving time.

Andy Owen, the director of advocacy communications at the National Association of Convenience Stores, said the association doesn’t take an official position on permanent daylight saving time “although we would be comfortable with it.”

“Shifting daylight to the end of the day tends to be good for business because it provides more time for shopping after regular work hours,” he said. “We want what’s good for businesses.”

Studies do support Trump’s argument that crime and accidents occur less with permanent daylight saving time. One study found that full-year daylight saving would reduce pedestrian fatalities by 13 percent and motor vehicle occupant fatalities by 3 percent.

Similarly, research has found that robberies drop about 7 percent for the entire day and 27 percent during the evening hour when sunlight is gained.

David Bieri, an associate professor at Virginia Tech, put together a brief on which states would benefit the most and least if daylight saving time was made permanent.

He found that permanent daylight saving time would pay off more in the north and on the eastern side of the time zones, like Seattle, Boston and Chicago.

“Permanent daylight time’s safety case is strongest in places like Boston and weakest in places like Indianapolis,” he said.

And while Trump said the twice-a-year clock change is “stress on people,” health associations like the American Academy of Sleep Medicine , the American Medical Association and the Society for Research on Biological Rhythms all say standard daylight time is better for health than daylight saving time.

“There’s the immediate hit and then there’s the slow burn,” Dr. Carla Finkielston, a professor with Virginia Tech’s Fralin Biomedical Research Institute, said of the health effects linked to the time changes.

“In the first few days after the spring change, researchers have reported shorter sleep, worse performance, a bump in heart attacks compared with neighboring weeks, and possibly more traffic accidents,” she said.

“The slow burn is the mismatch that sticks around, which we call social jetlag. Populations carrying more of that mismatch show higher rates of diabetes, obesity, heart disease, depression, and some cancers, along with shorter sleep and more trouble with mood and thinking.”

“The logic is simple enough. Standard Time is the arrangement where the clock on the wall sits closest to the sun overhead, so it asks the least of our biology,” she added.

While Trump has said the changing of the clocks is “a big inconvenience, and for our government, a VERY COSTLY EVENT,” studies have found that DST actually costs more.

Research from Chmura Economics & Analytics found that the total economic cost of DST in the U.S. is estimated at roughly $672.02 million annually, between lost productivity, injuries and accidents due to the sleep loss.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) doesn’t seem anxious to move on Trump’s daylight savings demands. He said earlier this month that there was no clear path for a successful vote on permanent daylight saving time in the Senate, despite the House passing the bill in a 308-117 vote.

Whether a Democratic majority would be inclined to make a change remains to be seen.

“The clock is shared infrastructure — a public good like weights and measures,” Bieri said. “When the evidence is a coin toss, Washington shouldn’t pick the option that once again favours the places that already have the most.”

articles.title: Feds ‘intensely’ probing alleged Alaska ballot scheme, US attorney confirms
articles.summary: Federal authorities are investigating whether Democrat Mary Peltola’s campaign’s reported effort to recruit a candidate in the Alaska Senate race with the same name as incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) violated the law, the state’s top federal prosecutor announced Friday. U.S. Attorney for the District of Alaska Michael Heyman said during a press conference that…
articles.body:
Federal authorities are investigating whether Democrat Mary Peltola’s campaign’s reported effort to recruit a candidate in the Alaska Senate race with the same name as incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) violated the law, the state’s top federal prosecutor announced Friday.

U.S. Attorney for the District of Alaska Michael Heyman said during a press conference that the investigation has been in the works for several months but that federal authorities are looking into the matter “intensely and swiftly” after “troubling new revelations” were reported by The New York Times this week.

The outlet reported Wednesday that Democratic operatives and Peltola’s campaign were involved in an effort to recruit a second Dan Sullivan to run in the state’s Senate race.

“This new information has resulted in a significant surge of law enforcement assets to Alaska, and I have assigned several attorneys in my office to assist in the matter as well,” Heyman said.

While the U.S. attorney would not disclose which potential crimes his office was looking into or whom it was targeting in the investigation, he emphasized a commitment to election security.

“What I can tell Alaskans is that we will not let anyone or any group undermine this election,” Heyman said.

Peltola, the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and the incumbent senator’s GOP challenger , Dan J. Sullivan, have all denied any involvement in the reported effort to recruit spoiler candidates for the race.

“I just want to clear the air: I knew nothing about any other candidate on the ballot except for me and the incumbent,” Peltola said during a Thursday evening speech in Juneau, Alaska. “That is all I have ever known about. I am not interested in tricking voters.”

This week, President Trump called for both Peltola and the spoiler candidate to be removed from the ballot and prosecuted . Additionally, Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy (R) on Wednesday ordered an investigation into Peltola over the Times’s reporting.

“Alaskans have a fundamental right to vote for the candidate they actually intend to support,” the Republican governor wrote on social media . “Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections.”

On Friday, Heyman urged anyone with knowledge about the “Dan Sullivan issue” or other potential election integrity violations to contact federal authorities.

“Within the last 24 hours or so, we have received a number of new pieces of information that we’re following up on,” he said. “Anybody with additional information should contact the FBI as soon as possible.”

In Iowa elections, cancer crisis looms large

Rising cancer rates and a potential link to farm pollution are causing a crisis in Iowa, throwing uncertainty into the midterm elections in the state that has shifted ruby red in recent years.

© Abel Uribe, Chicago Tribune, Tribune News Service via Getty Images file

Iowa suffers from the second-highest rate of new cancer cases in the U.S. and it’s one of the few states where the number of cancer cases are rising. Across the state, the cancer crisis has become a major campaign topic ahead of the midterm elections.

Candidates from both parties have made tackling the environmental causes of cancer—and blaming “Big Ag”— a key part of their platforms. It’s an attack that would have been unheard of from Republicans in the Corn Belt hub.

The state has a series of blockbuster races this year including the governor’s contest between Zach Lahn (R) and Rob Sand (D), the Senate race between Rep. Ashley Hinson (R) and state Rep. Josh Turek (D) as well as several competitive House seats.

Lahn, in an unusual move for a Republican, is embracing not only the cancer issue, but also vowing to clean the water and regulate chemicals if he’s elected.

These issues aren’t falling neatly along party lines and some Democrats are making the case that they’re best-suited to tackle the problem.

“This cancer issue is resonating with people and almost everyone has a story here of a family member or someone else that has met an early demise,” Democratic agriculture secretary candidate Chris Jones, who is emphasizing water quality in his campaign, told The Hill earlier this year.

articles.title: RNC chair predicts GOP wins in Alaska, Texas, 3 other battlegrounds

Gruters told NewsNation’s Blake Burman he expects Republicans will win Senate races in Maine, Texas, Ohio and Alaska — all of which…
articles.body:
Republican National Committee (RNC) Chair Joe Gruters remained optimistic Friday evening about his party’s chances in next week’s midterms, predicting big wins in key battleground states despite troubling polling numbers for the GOP.

Gruters told NewsNation’s Blake Burman he expects Republicans will win Senate races in Maine , Texas , Ohio and Alaska — all of which The Hill’s nonpartisan election forecasting partner, Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), lean “narrowly” toward Democrats. He also predicted a GOP victory in North Carolina , which the handicapper says will “likely” go blue.

Burman pressed the RNC chair on generic ballot polling that displayed a disadvantage for Republicans running this election cycle. An Emerson College Polling survey released Friday found Democrats held a 10-point lead over Republicans on a generic ballot.

“We put up candidates that can win and common-sense mainstream candidates, and I think that will make the difference,” Gruters told Burman. “So yes, maybe the generic ballot, we’re not doing so hot, but when it comes to candidates that are well known and they’re getting their message out, yes, we do have the benefit.”

DDHQ places the Democrats’ chances of regaining control of the House this November at 82 percent, according to a Friday forecast . The party has a slimmer chance at retaking the upper chamber of Congress, with the nonpartisan election handicapper placing this probability at around 62 percent.

The RNC chair also addressed President Trump’s reversal on his decision to cancel two rallies set for this weekend in Iowa and Kansas. The president announced Friday the events were back on and will both be held in person on Sunday.

“Listen, all these decisions are being made in real time,” Gruters said. “I mean, we’re looking at data, looking at where we may need to help certain candidates and people, and so there may be some more changes.”

Gruters also weighed in on Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy’s (R) response to reports that Democratic nominee Mary Peltola’s campaign was involved in an effort to recruit a candidate in the state’s Senate race with the same name as incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R).

When asked by Burman whether the RNC would seek to stall the certification of this election if Peltola was successful, Gruters said he would “follow the governor’s lead.”

“We’ll see [where] that investigation ends up, but we’re going to be ready to help any way we can,” he said.

On Friday, the top federal prosecutor in Alaska announced his office was involved in a separate investigation into whether any laws were broken in this alleged spoiler candidate effort. Peltola and her campaign have denied any involvement in the candidate’s recruitment.
